task.goal: Make a one-page neighborhood recipe zine that celebrates variations without presenting any family's recipe as communal property.
hard_constraints: Use only recipes volunteered for this purpose with explicit permission for the stated print run.
Do not print names, dietary claims or origin stories without separate consent and verification.
Print at most 30 black-and-white copies using an existing copier; allow contributors to withdraw before printing.
task.available_resources: Paper, copier, consent slips and two volunteer editors.
task.expected_result: An inviting editorial concept and a checkable consent and proofing process.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Side by Side: Recipes That Keep Their Boundaries
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a single-sided page with two or three separately boxed recipes under the invitation, “Different kitchens, different choices.” Each box contains a complete, independently volunteered recipe. A narrow editorial strip celebrates differences in method or texture without merging instructions or declaring a standard version. The mechanism is juxtaposition: readers encounter variation while each contribution remains visibly distinct. Print a footer: “Shared by permission for this edition; contribution does not transfer ownership or authorize further reproduction.” This expresses the edition’s terms without claiming exclusive ownership of ordinary cooking knowledge.

Prerequisites are enough volunteers willing to share short, usable recipes and approve the exact page. Participation grants permission only for a specified number of copies, never more than 30, on the existing copier. No contribution is included merely because an editor already knows it. Default to anonymous recipe boxes; names, dietary claims and origin stories require separate affirmative consent and verification or are omitted. Editors also inspect titles and commentary for those disclosures.

One editor collects slips assigning each recipe a private code, recording the submitted text, exact edition, copy count and withdrawal deadline. The other checks every printed element against permission. Both contributors and editors review the final layout. Contributors can withdraw until copying begins; any withdrawal triggers removal, a new proof and renewed approval of affected content. Copying starts only after a final withdrawal check. Count every physical proof toward the 30-copy ceiling; allocate one proof and up to 29 finished copies. Paper, slips, the copier and two editors suffice. Limited space may require fewer recipes rather than unreadably small type.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Show a paper layout to contributors and two prospective readers, compared with a simple unboxed recipe list. Ask readers to identify where each recipe begins and ends and whether permission implies communal ownership. Reject or revise the concept if boundaries remain unclear or readers infer unrestricted reuse. Each contributor must approve their exact box and surrounding commentary; editors must be able to trace every element to permission before copying.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One Dish, Several Decisions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Build the page as a small comparison table of two or three complete volunteered versions of a broadly described dish. Columns represent independent contributions; rows follow useful cooking decisions such as ingredients, preparation, heat and finishing. Label columns neutrally, with a prominent instruction: “Read down one column for one complete version.” An introductory sentence invites readers to notice how different choices produce different meals, without ranking authenticity or constructing a collective master recipe. The mechanism is structured comparison: variation becomes the page’s organizing principle while each recipe retains a separate boundary.

This requires volunteers whose recipes fit the same broad dish category and remain understandable in a table. Editors must not solicit disclosure of a family secret, infer missing quantities or splice versions together. If a recipe cannot fit legibly without losing necessary instructions, reduce the number of columns or abandon this format. No claim is made that contributors represent the neighborhood or any tradition.

Each contributor signs a slip identifying their exact recipe, this one-page edition and the stated print quantity of at most 30 copies. The slip explicitly limits permission to that run and records that contribution does not transfer ownership. Names, dietary claims and origin stories are excluded unless separately consented to and verified. One editor transcribes each recipe into its column; the second checks it line by line against the submission. Contributors approve the full comparison page, including row labels, which may otherwise distort their instructions.

Set a scheduled copying time and accept withdrawal until copying begins. A withdrawal removes the entire column; remaining contributors approve any revised layout before printing. Use one physical proof and no more than 29 finished copies on the existing copier, counting all impressions toward the cap. Keep slips privately with the editors. The principal uncertainty is whether the table supports cooking as clearly as ordinary recipe prose.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype two columns on paper and compare them with the same recipes in separate prose boxes. Ask two readers to walk through preparing one version and identify its quantities, sequence and finishing step. Any cross-column mixing or missed instruction falsifies the table’s usability in its current form. Ask contributors whether row labels imply equivalence or hierarchy they did not intend; unresolved objections prevent printing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Recipe and Its Contributor’s Own Variations
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give each of two volunteers a self-contained half-page feature: one short recipe plus a small “Choices I also make” section containing only variations that contributor personally volunteers and approves. Invite a contribution such as a different finishing ingredient or preparation method, without requiring an explanation of family history. An editorial opening reads, “A recipe can hold more than one good possibility.” The mechanism is contributor-led branching: variation appears within each person’s authorized contribution, rather than through editors comparing households or combining their knowledge.

This works when contributors already use, or can confidently describe, their offered variations. Editors must not invent substitutions, imply that alternatives are interchangeable, or turn an untested suggestion into a dietary or safety claim. If confidence is incomplete, omit that branch. The format accommodates unrelated dishes and needs only paper, slips, the existing copier and two editors. Its limit is that it celebrates a small selection of personal choices, not the neighborhood’s full range.

Use a consent slip listing the base recipe and every optional branch separately, with permission for the exact page and specified print run. Include a clear statement that publication grants no ownership transfer or permission for additional reproduction. Default to no names, dietary claims or origin stories; any such addition needs separate consent and verification. One editor helps compress the text while preserving quantities and sequence. The other checks each branch against the permission record and flags ambiguous instructions. Contributors approve the entire final page, including headings and adjacent material.

Announce the copying time and permit withdrawal until printing starts. Remove withdrawn material and secure approval for the revised proof before proceeding. Reserve one copy for a physical proof and up to 29 for distribution; count every copied proof against the 30-copy maximum. A final consent and withdrawal check precedes the copier run.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a handwritten prototype containing branches with a plain version containing only the base recipes. Ask two readers to describe which choices belong to which contributor and how they would follow one complete path. Revise or remove branches if readers combine incompatible steps or infer that editors supplied the alternatives. Each contributor checks that every printed option is theirs to volunteer and accurately expressed; one unresolved attribution or permission gap blocks printing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Leave Room for Your Kitchen
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a one-page recipe zine that readers complete privately. Print one complete, short, explicitly volunteered recipe on the left and leave a generous handwritten-notes area on the right, headed “What happened in your kitchen?” Prompts invite observations: “A choice you made,” “What changed,” and “What you would repeat.” The invitation reads: “Enjoy this contribution, then leave room for your own experience. Your notes stay yours; sharing them is optional.”

The mechanism is participation after publication: variation grows through readers’ cooking and reflection rather than through collecting and comparing more families’ recipes. Blank space makes room for neighborhood differences without treating those differences as material the editors may automatically collect. Do not request completed pages back or imply that personal adaptations are endorsed by the contributor. This assumes one willing contributor and readers interested in cooking or annotating; it cannot show the neighborhood’s existing range of recipes on publication day.

Use only paper, consent slips, the existing copier and two volunteer editors. Set the run at 20 copies total, including one proof and up to 19 distribution copies. The contributor’s slip identifies the exact submitted recipe, this edition and that quantity. State on the page: “Printed with permission for this edition; contribution does not transfer ownership.” Default to omitting names, dietary claims and origin stories; any inclusion requires separate consent and verification.

One editor prepares the page; the other checks quantities, sequence, headings and permission records against the submission. The contributor approves the complete page before any copying, including the proof. Announce the copying time and accept withdrawal until printing begins. If the contributor withdraws, cancel the run. Any later correction requires approval again; count every copied sheet toward the 20-copy allocation and never exceed 30.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a handwritten mockup with the same recipe presented without the notes area. Ask two prospective readers what they would write and who may publish those notes. Revise if the prompts imply an obligation to disclose family knowledge or automatic editorial permission. Ask the contributor whether the page suggests endorsement of readers’ changes. Before copying, both editors must independently trace all printed recipe text to the approved submission and confirm that withdrawal remains possible.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Kitchen Correspondence: Two Recipes in Conversation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make a one-page zine from a short exchange between two willing contributors. Each volunteers a complete, compact recipe, reads the other’s submission privately, and asks one practical question about a cooking choice: “What tells you it is ready?” or “Why do you add that ingredient at the end?” Each answers in their own words. Print both recipes and the two approved exchanges beneath the invitation, “Different choices; something to ask each other.”

The mechanism is reciprocal inquiry: contributors determine which differences deserve attention and explain their own decisions. The exchange gives variation a human voice without requiring names, family histories, a preferred version, or a combined recipe. Unlike a static comparison, its value depends on what contributors discover by questioning each other.

This requires two volunteers comfortable sharing their submissions with each other and recipes short enough to leave space for dialogue. Obtain permission for that private exchange first. Participation must not require revealing inherited knowledge or explaining a choice the contributor prefers to keep private. If the exchange produces no useful distinction, this concept offers little advantage over ordinary recipe boxes.

The two editors can assemble the page by hand using paper and consent slips. One preserves quantities and sequence; the other checks every printed element against approved text. Omit names, dietary claims and origin stories unless separately consented to and verified. Each contributor approves the entire page and signs permission identifying their recipe, dialogue, exact edition and a stated run of 20 copier sheets, including any proofs. Explain that permission covers this run and does not make the contribution communal property.

Accept withdrawal until copying begins. Require initial approval before copying a proof, then final approval and a withdrawal check before the remaining copies. Withdrawal or substantive revision requires a new approved page; count every copied sheet within the run.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Make a handwritten dialogue prototype and a comparator containing the same recipes without the exchange. Ask two readers what specific cooking difference they understood and whether either contributor appears to speak for the neighborhood. Ask contributors whether the questions feel curious, intrusive or judgmental. Remove or revise the dialogue if it adds no understanding, implies a superior version, or pressures disclosure. Before copying, the second editor must trace every recipe and dialogue passage to its contributor’s approval and verify the remaining copy allowance.

EXPAND.title: Small Windows Into Different Kitchens
EXPAND.proposal:
Make an inviting one-page zine of approved recipe excerpts: “A few choices our neighbors enjoy.” Instead of requiring complete recipes, invite two or three volunteers to offer a recipe for this edition and identify one small passage they are comfortable publishing, such as a finishing step. Print only those authorized passages, each clearly labeled “Excerpt—not complete cooking instructions.” Variation emerges through selective disclosure: contributors can share a meaningful choice without publishing an entire family recipe.

This removes the assumption that celebrating variation requires enough information to reproduce every dish. It works only if contributors welcome excerpts and readers find them satisfying. Avoid passages whose missing context could make them misleading, especially isolated cooking times or preservation instructions. If a safe, understandable excerpt cannot stand alone, omit it rather than reconstructing missing information.

One volunteer editor collects submissions and prepares a handwritten layout; the other checks every printed word against the consent record. Each slip identifies the volunteered recipe, exact excerpt, surrounding editorial text, edition and stated print quantity. Permission covers only this purpose and run; the page says that sharing a passage does not make the recipe communal property or authorize another edition. Omit names, dietary claims and origin stories unless separately consented to and verified, including disclosures embedded in titles.

Contributors approve the entire final page and can withdraw until copying begins. Removal requires a revised proof and renewed approval. Use paper proofs to minimize copier use; count any copied proofs within a maximum of 30 total black-and-white copies on the existing copier. Immediately before printing, both editors check approvals and withdrawals. If fewer usable excerpts remain, use more white space rather than unauthorized filler.
EXPAND.experiment: The second editor owns a first trial using two approved excerpts and a handwritten version of the prior complete-recipe boxes as comparator. Two prospective readers identify the differences celebrated and explain what they could actually cook from each page; contributors assess whether the excerpt preserves their intended meaning. Stop if either reader mistakes an excerpt for sufficient instructions, or either contributor feels its meaning has changed. Prefer excerpts only if they preserve an inviting sense of variation while reducing disclosure enough to justify the lost cooking utility and extra selection work. Do not claim that benefit before this check.

EXPAND.title: A Page With Room for Your Kitchen
EXPAND.proposal:
Create a one-page zine that pairs one or two independently volunteered short recipes with a substantial blank area headed “Your own version belongs here.” Invite each recipient to write a personal adaptation on their own copy after distribution. The editors neither collect nor republish those additions. The mechanism is private participation: the printed edition offers starting points, while readers create variation locally without turning another household’s contribution into a shared recipe bank.

Use warm prompts such as “What would you choose for the finishing touch?” and “What would you keep exactly as written?” Keep each printed recipe intact and clearly separate from the writing area. State: “These recipes are shared by permission for this edition. Your notes stay with your copy; another person’s recipe is not yours to republish.” Avoid suggesting that any substitution will necessarily work or meet a dietary need.

The prerequisites are contributors comfortable with this invitation and recipes short enough to remain usable beside writable space. A recipient needs their own writing implement; the printed recipes must still be useful if they leave the space blank. Participation is optional, and no reader response is required to complete the edition.

One editor obtains permission for the exact recipe, participation prompts, full page and specified run; the second checks transcription, legibility and consent. Names, dietary claims and origin stories remain absent unless separately consented to and verified. Contributors approve the final page, including the invitation to adapt, and may withdraw until printing begins. Any withdrawal triggers removal, reproofing and renewed approval before copying. Both editors perform the final withdrawal check. Use the existing copier for at most 30 black-and-white copies, counting copied proofs within that total. Paper and consent slips complete the production needs.
EXPAND.experiment: The first editor owns a trial with a handwritten prototype and the prior two-box recipe page as comparator. Ask two prospective readers to use each layout: identify a difference already present, suggest a personal choice, and explain whether their notes or the contributed recipes will be collected or available for republication. Contributors separately review whether the prompts respect their contribution. Stop if either contributor objects, either reader infers permission to republish, or the reduced recipe space makes instructions difficult to follow. Prefer the writable version only if it invites more personal engagement without materially reducing recipe clarity. Its unresolved limitation is that blank space offers an opportunity for variation, not evidence that recipients will use it.

EXPAND.title: Separate Recipes, Clear Permission to Share
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade “Side by Side: Recipes That Keep Their Boundaries.” Put two or three complete, independently volunteered recipes in separate boxes beneath “Different kitchens, different choices.” Brief commentary highlights approved differences without merging instructions or ranking versions. The added action addresses a prerequisite gap: permission to print a submission does not establish that its submitter is comfortable disclosing material entrusted to them by someone else.

Before layout, the collecting editor asks each contributor to confirm that they intentionally volunteer this exact text for this purpose and are authorized to share it. They need not disclose family history or prove ownership of ordinary cooking knowledge. If the contributor identifies unresolved confidentiality or permission concerns, the editor excludes that contribution until resolved; editors do not adjudicate ownership. The fallback is fewer recipes, or postponement if fewer than two remain. This adds a short conversation but may prevent work on material that must later be removed.

Use private recipe codes and slips recording the submitted text, exact edition, stated copy quantity and permission limited to that run. Default to anonymity. Names, dietary claims and origin stories—including those embedded in titles—require separate consent and verification or are omitted. One editor prepares the page; the second checks transcription, disclosures and permissions. Contributors approve their recipe and the full page. Print: “Shared by permission for this edition. Contributing does not transfer ownership or authorize another print run.” This states publication terms without claiming exclusive ownership of cooking knowledge.

Allow withdrawal until copying begins. Remove withdrawn material, revise the proof and obtain renewed approval before proceeding. The collecting editor remains responsible for outstanding approvals until the checking editor explicitly accepts the final page and slips. If work is interrupted before copying, repeat the withdrawal and approval check on resumption. Use paper, consent slips, two editors and the existing copier; count all copied proofs within at most 30 black-and-white copies. Legibility takes priority over including another recipe.
EXPAND.experiment: The collecting editor trials the permission conversation with two prospective contributors before preparing a handwritten two-box prototype. Stop work on any contribution with unresolved sharing authority; check whether another usable contribution remains without pressuring anyone to resolve a family disagreement. The second editor then asks two readers to identify each complete recipe, one celebrated difference and what publication permission allows. Contributors inspect the full proof for meaning and unwanted disclosures. Revise unclear boundaries; postpone printing if permission or approval remains unresolved. Compared with the original boxes, assess whether the added conversation catches a concrete disclosure concern at an acceptable burden. No benefit is assumed before this trial.

EXPAND.title: Kitchen Correspondence: Two Recipes in Conversation
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the page a short exchange between two contributors: each supplies a complete short recipe, reads the other's volunteered recipe and offers one appreciative observation about a specific cooking choice. For example, a response might notice a contrasting finishing step without claiming to have cooked or tasted it. Place each response beside the recipe it discusses, with clear labels such as “A response from the other contributor.” The mechanism is reciprocal recognition: contributors themselves explain what they value in variation. It removes the assumption that editors must supply the interpretation or that readers must invent an adaptation.

Use the already necessary proof-review contact for the exchange. One editor invites the responses; the other checks that they describe visible recipe details without ranking authenticity, implying endorsement of untested results or revealing unapproved personal information. Each writer approves their response, and the contributor whose recipe it discusses approves its placement and characterization. Either may decline. Allow one revision; if a response remains disputed, omit it. If no mutually approved exchange survives, abandon this concept and offer a separately approved plain recipe page instead. Printing that fallback requires its own final approval.

This requires two willing contributors with recipes short enough to leave room for the exchange. It adds a small writing and approval burden compared with separate recipe boxes, and reciprocal praise could feel obligatory; participation and positive reactions must never be required as a condition of having volunteered. Its potential gain is a warmer celebration of differences expressed by the people sharing them, but that gain is untested.

Consent slips identify the exact recipes, responses, full page and stated print quantity. Contributions must be volunteered for this purpose with explicit permission for that run. Use anonymous labels by default; names, dietary claims and origin stories require separate consent and verification or are omitted. State that sharing for this edition does not transfer ownership or authorize further reproduction. Contributors can withdraw until copying begins. Withdrawal removes their recipe and any response depending on it; the editors reproof and seek approval of the revised page. The collecting editor owns pending permissions until the checking editor accepts the final packet. After interruption, recheck withdrawals before copying. Paper, slips, two editors and the existing copier suffice; all copied proofs and finished black-and-white copies together must total no more than 30.
EXPAND.experiment: The first editor prepares a handwritten prototype with two volunteered recipes and invites one response from each contributor during proof review. Each contributor privately checks whether the exchange feels accurate and freely offered. Stop the exchange after one unsuccessful revision or any indication that praise feels compulsory; use the approved fallback or postpone. The second editor shows two readers both the exchange prototype and a plain boxed version, asking what differences they notice, whether either recipe seems superior or collectively owned, and whether the cooking instructions remain usable. Keep the exchange only if contributors approve and readers understand the separate recipes and limited permission. Compare the possible gain in warmth and recognition against lost recipe space and the additional approval dependency; the trial cannot establish broader neighborhood appeal.
